1 big thing: Apple's "nothing broken" quarter
By Nathan Bomey and Bradley Olson
 

Apple CEO John Ternus. Photo: Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images
 

Apple delivered higher revenue than expected last quarter as the tech giant rides an uptick in iPhone sales but apparently disappointed investors with its outlook for the December period.

By the numbers: The world's newly recrowned most valuable company posted revenue of $114.5 billion, up 11.7% compared to a year earlier.

  • That topped S&P Capital IQ consensus expectations of $113.4 billion.

📈 The intrigue: Apple's cautious approach to AI spending has been growing on investors, with its stock up about 25% in 2026.

🤖 Catch up quick: Today's earnings report marks the first for John Ternus in his new role as CEO after he took the reins from Tim Cook, who is now executive chair.

  • Investors are awaiting clues on how Ternus will guide Apple's AI strategy moving forward.

📱 💻 Zoom in: The company sold 57.58 million iPhones and 10.79 million Macs in the period, up 17.5% and 23.7%, respectively, from a year earlier.

  • Sales in Apple's services business, which helped sustain its valuation in recent years under Cook's leadership, rose by almost 10%.
  • In China, a key sales region for the company, Apple saw a sharp increase in revenue relative to somewhat tepid gains in recent years. Revenue from Greater China rose by more than 20% to $17.5 billion.

🤷 Yes, but: Apple fell about 4% in after-hours trading after the company guided growth in the December quarter between 7% and 10% year over year, citing supply constraints.

🗣️ What they're saying: "There's nothing broken in this quarter, but there wasn't enough here to move the story forward either," writes Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion. "Apple delivered the records traders expected but the stock's reaction says the recent move higher was already doing a lot of the work."

2. 🏃 Marvell gains Lumentum
 
Data: Financial Modeling Prep; Chart: Dan Primack/Axios

Marvell Technology today announced that it will buy optical components maker Lumentum for $115 billion in stock.

  • It's the largest merger ever between public tech companies — and a major vote of confidence in the AI data center boom, Axios' Dan Primack writes.

🥧 Between the lines: The value of this deal isn't primarily in cost savings (though the companies say they see a path to plenty of those), but in combining complementary technologies to capture a bigger slice of the AI spending pie, Goldman analysts wrote last week before the deal was confirmed, Axios' Pete Gannon writes.

  • Marvell makes chips, while Lumentum specializes in the lasers and optical technologies that help move data between them using light.
  • The bet is that bringing those capabilities under one roof will create a new kind of AI infrastructure supplier. "We are going to create a new category of company here," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC.

📉 What we're watching: Investors will need some convincing — Marvell shares fell nearly 13% today. Lumentum slipped almost 19%.

The bottom line: Investors are increasingly worried about the sustainability of the AI spending boom. Almost as worried as they are about missing out on it.

3. Other happenings

4. 🎸 Rewind and cash in
 

Gerard Way of My Chemical Romance performs "Welcome to the Black Parade" in 2006. Photo: Theo Wargo/WireImage
 

We'll forgive you for thinking it's 2006 when you glance at the Billboard 200 this week.

  • My Chemical Romance is topping the charts for the first time with a special edition re-release of its 20-year-old album "The Black Parade," AP reports.

🎧 State of play: The rock opera album — which couldn't top Disney's "Hannah Montana" on the charts two decades ago, coming in at No. 2 — sold the equivalent of 78,000 album units in the U.S. last week, according to Luminate.

  • It's benefiting from a creative release strategy that involved 20 physical variants and six bonus tracks.

💭 Nathan's thought bubble: I suspect we'll see more retro music being re-released — in the same way that old movies are also having a moment in the theater — as stressed-out people pine for better days from the past.
